name: Mental Maths: 3-Digit × 1-Digit Multiplication
description: KaTeX-enabled practice for three-digit by one-digit multiplication: chunking, full partial products, doubling, ×5, ×9, nearby bases, estimation, error checks, and strategy selection.
estimatedTime: 140–175 minutes for a first focused pass; then 10–15 minute review bursts

cards.definition:
Split into hundreds, tens, and ones.

$$
\begin{aligned}
468\times7 \\
&=2800+420+56 \\
&=3276
\end{aligned}
$$
Keep full partial products rather than carrying individual digits.

For 786 × 6, think 4200 + 480 + 36, not a chain of carry digits.

$$
\begin{aligned}
786\times6 \\
&=4200+480+36 \\
&=4716
\end{aligned}
$$

Double twice.

$$
\begin{aligned}
368\times2&=736 \\
736\times2&=1472
\end{aligned}
$$

Double three times.

$$
\begin{aligned}
157\times2&=314 \\
314\times2&=628 \\
628\times2&=1256
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply by 10, then halve.

$$
\begin{aligned}
346\times5 \\
&=3460\div2 \\
&=1730
\end{aligned}
$$

Use 9 = 10 − 1.

$$
\begin{aligned}
367\times9 \\
&=3670-367 \\
&=3303
\end{aligned}
$$

Round the 3-digit number to a nearby hundred.

683 × 7 ≈ 700 × 7 = 4900. The exact answer should be in that region.

cards.term: 3-Digit × 1-Digit: When is a nearby base useful?
cards.definition:
When the correction is small.

$$
\begin{aligned}
299\times6 \\
&=(300-1)\times6 \\
&=1800-6 \\
&=1794
\end{aligned}
$$

Repeated doubling.

$$
\begin{aligned}
384\times2&=768 \\
768\times2&=1536
\end{aligned}
$$

Use 9 = 10 − 1.

$$
\begin{aligned}
673\times9 \\
&=6730-673 \\
&=6057
\end{aligned}
$$

cards.term: 3-Digit × 1-Digit: When should you use ordinary chunking?
cards.definition:
When no special multiplier or base gives a clearly shorter route.

$$
\begin{aligned}
462\times7 \\
&=400\times7+60\times7+2\times7 \\
&=2800+420+14 \\
&=3234
\end{aligned}
$$
Estimate the size and check the last digit. For 468 × 7, the answer should be near 3500 and end in 6. 3276 passes both checks.

cards.term: Which estimate is better for 683 × 7: 3400, 4800, or 9000?

cards.term: True or false: n × 8 can always be found by doubling n three times.
cards.definition: True, because 8 = 2 × 2 × 2.
